title: An Alternative Model of Laser-Induced Stroke in the Motor Cortex of Rats
author: Boyko, Kuts, et al.
materials: Data of interest will be made available on request.

steps.title: Obtain ethical approval
steps.instruction: Confirm that the study complies with the Declaration of Helsinki, the Tokyo guidelines, and the European Community animal‑use regulations, and obtain approval from the Ben‑Gurion University Animal Care Committee.

steps.title: Acquire and house animals
steps.instruction: Purchase 210 male Sprague‑Dawley rats (300–350 g, Harlan Laboratories, Israel). House three rats per cage for at least three days for acclimatization. Provide ad libitum Purina chow and water.

steps.title: Assign rats to experimental groups
steps.instruction: Randomly allocate 120 rats to the laser arm and 90 rats to the MCAO arm. In the MCAO arm, assign 30 rats each to transient (MCAO‑t) and permanent (MCAO‑p) subgroups and 30 to a sham control (anesthesia + skin incision only). Anticipate 17 % and 20 % mortality in MCAO‑t and MCAO‑p, leaving 25 and 24 rats respectively. In the laser arm, assign 20 rats each to five power‑dose subgroups (25X1, 50X1, 50X2, 50X5, 50X10 J) and 20 to a sham control; mortality is 0 %, so numbers remain unchanged.

steps.title: Perform modified ICA MCAO surgery
steps.instruction: Anesthetize rats with 2 % isoflurane in oxygen, allow spontaneous breathing, and maintain core temperature at 37 °C using a rectal temperature‑regulated heating pad. Under aseptic conditions, make a midline neck incision, expose the right common carotid artery (CCA) from bifurcation to skull base, isolate and coagulate the occipital artery and external carotid artery (ECA) branches, then dissect the ECA distally and coagulate it together with terminal lingual and maxillary branches. Insert a catheter via the ECA stump directly through the internal carotid artery (ICA) to the MCA, secure a 4‑0 silk filament over the ECA, and loosely tie a 4‑0 silk suture around the ICA proximal to the filament to occlude the ICA. Close the incision with surgical sutures, discontinue anesthesia, and allow recovery. Total surgery time ≈ 25–30 min.

steps.title: Induce laser stroke
steps.instruction: Anesthetize rats with 2 % isoflurane in oxygen, maintain core temperature at 37 °C with a rectal heating pad, and place the animal prone on a stereotaxic head holder. Make a 3 cm scalp incision, reflect the skin laterally, and expose the skull between Bregma and Lambda; mark the target sites. Position a Sharplan 3000 Nd‑YAG laser 2 mm above the exposed cortex. Deliver the prescribed energy to the right hemisphere: 25 J × 1 pulse, 50 J × 1 pulse, 50 J × 2 pulses, 50 J × 5 pulses, or 50 J × 10 pulses, each pulse lasting 1 s. Ensure laser power does not exceed 50 J per second to avoid bone damage. After irradiation, close the scalp with sutures, discontinue anesthesia, and return the rat to its cage. Total procedure time ≈ 5 min.

steps.title: Neurological deficit screening (NSS)
steps.instruction: One hour after stroke induction, assess each rat on a 0–4 motor‑deficit scale (0 = no deficit; 1 = forelimb flexion; 2 = weak contralateral forelimb grip; 3 = circling when tail‑pulled; 4 = spontaneous circling). Discard rats scoring 0. Test the remaining rats with the full 43‑parameter Neurological Severity Score (range 0–43).

steps.title: Euthanize and collect brains
steps.instruction: Twenty‑four hours after the procedure, euthanize rats by inhalation of high‑flow CO₂, then decapitate. Rapidly isolate the brain. For each subgroup (Naïve, MCAO‑t, MCAO‑p, Laser 25X1, 50X1, 50X2, 50X5, 50X10) select ten randomly chosen rats for downstream analyses.

steps.title: Measure infarct volume (TTC staining)
steps.instruction: Slice each brain into six coronal sections, each 2 mm thick. Incubate sections for 30 min at 37 °C in 0.05 % 2,3,5‑triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC). Scan sections with a Canon Cano Scan 4200F scanner at 1600 × 1600 dpi. Define unstained areas as infarcted, quantify pixel area with ImageJ 1.37v, and express infarct size as a percentage of the contralateral (uninjured) hemisphere. Correct for swelling using: corrected infarct = (infarct × contralateral hemisphere size) / (ipsilateral hemisphere size).

steps.title: Assess brain edema extent
steps.instruction: Using the same scanned TTC images, calculate the pixel‑based volume of the right and left hemispheres with ImageJ 1.37v. Compute edema percentage with the Kaplan method: edema = [(right hemisphere volume – left hemisphere volume) / left hemisphere volume] × 100 %.

steps.title: Determine BBB breakage (Evans Blue assay)
steps.instruction: Inject Evans Blue dye (2 % in saline, 4 ml kg⁻¹) intravenously via the tail vein and allow circulation for 60 min. Perfuse each rat through the left ventricle with cooled saline at 110 mmHg until the outflow from the right atrium is clear. Remove the brain, cut it into 2‑mm coronal slices, separate left and right hemispheres, and weigh each slice.

steps.title: Process tissue for Evans Blue quantification
steps.instruction: Weigh each brain region, homogenize in 1 ml of 50 % trichloroacetic acid (w/v), and centrifuge at 10 000 × g for 20 min. Mix 1 ml of supernatant with 1.5 ml of solvent (50 % TCA : 96 % ethanol, 1 : 3). Measure fluorescence on a Tecan Infinite 200 PRO multimode reader (excitation 620 nm ± 10 nm; emission 680 nm ± 10 nm). Quantify Evans Blue concentration using external standards ranging from 10 to 500 ng ml⁻¹. Express results as mean ± SD in mg g⁻¹ protein.

steps.title: Data handling and availability
steps.instruction: Compile all measurements (body temperature, mortality, NSS scores, infarct volume, edema, BBB breakage, etc.) and store them securely. Data of interest will be made available on request.

description: Compared to original MCAO permanent or transient techniques, the model of laser-induced stroke demonstrated neither mortality nor SAH, findings that are favorable with the minimally invasive method we used. We can expect that null level of SAH and low mortality rate will be the rule for the laser model. The reason for this assumption is that the main cause of SAH and death in the MCAO induced stroke is tearing of a blood vessel and subsequent intracranial pressure (ICP) elevation. The laser impact on the brain tissue does not include direct blood vessel intervention and also causes coagulation, leading to a minimal risk of blood vessel tearing in the laser model. Additionally, as our findings suggest, laser-induced stroke causes less brain edema and less ICP elevation than the MCAO induced stroke, which also positively impacts the survival rates. Temperature elevation was almost absent in rats with laser-induced stroke in comparison to rats with MCAO induced stroke, and the temperature variability at the laser subgroups was lower. The reason for these findings is that the laser method is relatively minimally invasive and does not cause hypothalamic artery occlusion, which often happens during the MCAO procedure and causes impairment of the hypothalamus function which includes the temperature control [8]. The low variability of the laser method was a consistent finding of our study and was also supported by the results of stroke size and extent of brain edema. Compared to the MCAO-p subgroup there was both less histological damage and less variability than in laser subgroups. The important finding of our study is that the impact of a laser can be less, the same, or even more than that of the artery occlusion, depending on the induced power, but the dispersion of its impact between different rats stays consistently lower.
